column2: A slate reads nine. Someone is rewriting it as ten. Glance at it mid-stroke, and you might read nine, or ten, or, Lamport says, two thousand four hundred ninety-six.
Could computers take turns safely with memory like that? In nineteen seventy-three, that was considered impossible.
Two programs, running at once, share a scoreboard that reads forty-one. Programmers write x equals x plus one. It isn't an equation. It means make x one bigger.
That's two steps. Read the score, then write it back plus one.
Here's one unlucky order. Both read forty-one, and both write forty-two. Two points scored, one counted.
Draw every order at once, as staircases from corner to corner. There are six. How many lose a point?
Four. Exactly the ones through the middle, where both have read and neither has written. The fix has to wall off the middle.
Counting orders isn't measuring chances. Each program usually runs both steps back to back, so in a real machine the bad orders are rare. But at billions of steps a second, rare means constantly.
The fix seems obvious. Only one program at a time may touch the scoreboard. Call that stretch of code the room.
Put a sign on the door. Check that it says vacant, flip it to occupied, and go in.
Does the sign work?
No. Both read vacant before either flips it. Of the fourteen orders, eight put both in the room at once.
Edsger Dijkstra posed the problem properly in nineteen sixty-five. Never two in the room. Someone who wanders off outside can't block everyone. And fast or slow, it still works.
A year later, Donald Knuth asked for more. Everyone who wants in gets in eventually.

Hardware usually cheats, with a magic sign you can check and flip in one motion. Dijkstra showed that ordinary signs are enough, several of them used cleverly, as long as nobody can catch one halfway through a flip.
Now a harder question. What if a glance can catch a sign mid-flip, as a blur? Hold that thought.
Picture a bakery. Take a number, and the lowest number is served next. From now on, each program is a customer, and being served means going into the room.
But a ticket machine is shared. Two customers pressing at once could get the same ticket, just like the lost point. It would need a room of its own.
So each customer gets her own slate, and only she writes on it. A zero means not in line.
To take a ticket, read every other slate, one at a time, and write one more than the biggest. Blue reads three, zero, zero, two. What does she write?
Four. Then she waits until nobody with a smaller ticket is still in line. Here that's Pink, with two, then Green, with three, then Blue.
Whoever is in the room plays their own tune, so only one tune sounds at a time.
No shared ticket machine. Nobody ever writes on anyone else's slate.
Can two customers get the same ticket?
Yes. Before anyone is served, Purple and Teal read the slates at the same moment. Both see four as the biggest, and both write five.
If equal tickets both go in, both end up in the room. Change the rule to wait for anyone with a smaller or equal ticket, and they both wait, bowing to each other forever. After you. No, after you.
The fix is a tie-breaker. Compare tickets, and if they're equal, the lower customer number goes first, like a dictionary. Purple is three and Teal is four, so Purple goes first.
Put every ticket on a grid, ticket across and customer number up, and sweep column by column. Blue holds ticket three. Teal holds ticket two. Who goes first?
Teal. A customer with the lowest number still waits for every smaller ticket. The number only breaks ties. That's the order in which the room takes everyone holding a ticket.
The second crack is sneakier. Blue reads Green's slate, sees zero, and decides on ticket one. But she hasn't written it yet.
Green takes ticket one, checks Blue's slate, sees zero, which means not in line, and walks in.
Then Blue writes her one, sees a tie, wins it on her lower number, and walks in too. Both in the room.
The fix is a flag that says, I'm choosing, don't judge me yet. Raise it before reading, and lower it after writing. Before comparing with someone, wait until their flag is down.
Same unlucky order, now with flags. What does Green do this time?
She sees Blue's flag up, and waits.
Without flags, two customers visiting once have twenty-eight possible orders, and four put both in the room. With flags, there are three hundred twenty-two, and not one does.
The time your flag is up is your choosing time. The flag isn't a lock. Nobody waits to raise their own, and many can be up at once.
So the gap between looking and writing is still there. The flag makes it visible, and the tie-breaker settles equal tickets.
Now take three customers. The square becomes a cube. How many orders are there now?
Over two billion. And not one of them puts two in the room.
Here's one full run, fast.
Purple and Green arrive together, and both choose ticket one. Purple finishes first and finds Green's flag still up, so she waits. Without the flag, she'd have read Green's unwritten ticket as zero.
Teal sees one and one. What ticket does she take?
Two. And the tie between Purple and Green goes to Green, the lower number.
Blue arrives late, with the lowest number, and takes three. She waits for Purple, then Teal. Green leaves, gets back in line, and takes four. Who's served first follows the grid exactly.
Why can two customers never be in the room at once? Picture Blue inside, and Green holding a ticket.
Fact one. If Blue finished choosing before Green started, and still holds that ticket, then Green's ticket is bigger. Green saw Blue's.
Fact two. If Blue is in the room, everyone else holding a ticket has a bigger pair than hers. Why is that true?
Take the last time Blue checked Green's flag, the check that let her through. Where could Green have been?
Three places. Not yet choosing. Then by fact one, Green's ticket will be bigger.
In the middle of choosing. Then Green's flag was up, and that check wouldn't have let Blue through.
Finished choosing. Then Blue read Green's real ticket, and went in only because her pair was smaller. Either way, Green's pair is bigger. That's fact two.
Now suppose both were in the room. Then fact two says each one's pair is smaller than the other's. Like being taller than you, and you taller than me. Impossible.
A computer search agrees, over every order, up to four customers, as long as tickets stay small. But a search only covers small cases. The proof covers all of them.
Remember the slate caught mid-stroke? Rewrite oh-nine as ten one digit at a time, and a glance in between reads nineteen, or zero zero.
Lamport went further. A glance during a write may return any number the slate could hold. Even two thousand four hundred ninety-six.
Twelve years later he named memory like that safe. A funny name, since it's the least safe kind.
Back to the proof picture. Let every slate and every flag flicker while it's written. Does the proof ever trust a ticket read that crosses a write?
Never. It trusts just two ticket reads. Green reading Blue's finished ticket, and Blue reading Green's finished ticket. Nobody was writing either slate.
A glance that catches garbage, say seven, just makes a customer take eight and wait longer.
And a glance that catches Blue's old zero mid-write lets Green straight in. Is that dangerous?
No. Green had already seen Blue's flag down, and nobody writes a ticket with the flag down. So Blue started choosing after Green finished. By fact one, Blue's ticket will be bigger, so Blue waits.
Lamport noticed this only after writing the proof. In his words, the read may return any arbitrary value. His colleague Anatol Holt refused to believe it.

One caution, from Lamport himself. Find the biggest ticket by reading each slate exactly once. The obvious loop reads a slate twice, once to compare and once to copy, and a flicker between them can break it.
It's also fair. Finish choosing your ticket before I start choosing mine, and you're served first. If we were choosing at the same time, either of us may go first.

So nobody waits forever, as long as everyone in the room eventually leaves, and nobody stalls for good with a raised flag or a ticket. Once you've taken your ticket, each other customer can get ahead of you at most once.
The price is that tickets keep growing as long as somebody is always in line. They reset only when the bakery empties.
Lamport did the sum. At one customer a millisecond, how big do the tickets get in a year?
Still below about thirty-four billion, two to the thirty-five. That's too big for a thirty-two bit number, which would wrap in under two months.
A sixty-four bit number lasts centuries, even at a billion tickets a second. As long as a glance never returns more than was ever written.
And it isn't cheap. Even alone, a customer makes three reads for every other customer. One customer frozen while choosing stalls everyone.
The proof is right. But run this on your laptop as written, and it can fail, because your laptop breaks one of the proof's promises.
Your laptop has several processors, called cores. Picture each one running a customer. Each core drops its writes in an outbox and keeps going.
Both customers raise their flags and write their tickets, into their outboxes. Then each reads the other's slate. What does it see?
No flag. Both walk in, while the real slates still say nobody is even choosing.

The fix is a fence. Wait until your outbox is delivered before reading anyone else's slate. On an Intel or AMD chip, two fences each time you enter are enough, one after raising your flag, and one after lowering it.
Arm chips, like the ones in recent Macs, reorder even more, so they need more care.
The easy, correct way everywhere is sequentially consistent atomics. Acquire and release are not enough here, because this needs your write to land before your next read.
In practice, people use the hardware's magic signs, called atomic instructions. So does the bakery still run anywhere?

Yes. In Arm's own reference firmware, in the code that runs while a core wakes up with its data cache still off. Until it rejoins the others, the usual spinlocks can't be used, so it takes a ticket, bakery style.

And its trick of taking a ticket bigger than any you've seen, with numbers to break ties, reappears in how Lamport later ordered events across whole networks. It's in the ballot numbers of Paxos too, the method that keeps copies of a database agreeing.
Lamport says he didn't invent the bakery algorithm. He discovered it. It just seemed to come out of thin air, and perhaps, he says, that's why he's proudest of it.
